description: CODEV - Alpha is building an interactive web application that uses advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data to track and visualize changes on Earth's surface. By turning complex satellite radar signals into clear, user-friendly maps and time-series dashboards, our tool helps researchers and communities monitor environmental changes like floods, deforestation, and land movement—day or night, and through any weather.
summary:
Every rainy season the Mekong River pushes water backwards into Tonle Sap, Cambodia's great lake. The lake grows about five times in size and floods the surrounding forest, which becomes the nursery for one of the world's largest inland fisheries. That flooded forest is shrinking and the yearly flood is weakening, yet it is hard to see from space: clouds block cameras, and the water hides under the trees.
We built an open-source interactive story map from 11 NISAR L-band radar images (19 June – 29 October 2026, mostly one every 12 days). NISAR's long waves pass through the canopy and bounce off the water and tree trunks (a "double bounce"), revealing flooded forest that cameras miss. On 30 August the flooded forest stood out from the surrounding trees by 2.3 dB in NISAR but only 0.8 dB in Sentinel-1. The HH channel captured the change, while HV barely moved.
What we found (40 × 40 km on the north shore, near Siem Reap):
* Flooded forest grew about 8× by 30 August (39 → 311 km²).
* Open water grew 72% by 17 October (611 → 1,050 km²).
* The hidden flood under the trees peaked 5–7 weeks before the open-water flood.
Users can play through the season, compare dates and click any spot to see its history. Repeated each year with free NISAR data, these maps could flag weak-flood years for fisheries managers, forest protection teams and disaster agencies.
details:
What it does
The Invisible Flood is an interactive web story map that shows how Cambodia’s Tonle Sap lake floods its forest each rainy season, including the part of the flood hidden under the trees and under monsoon clouds. It turns 11 NISAR radar images into maps, an animation and charts that anyone can explore.

How it works

  1. We downloaded NISAR Level-2 GCOV products (track 083 ascending, frame 008, 20 m, HH + HV) from NASA’s ASF DAAC with the earthaccess library, reading only our 40 × 40 km window from each ~3 GB file.
  2. We averaged pixels to 100 m cells in linear power to reduce radar speckle, then converted to decibels.
  3. Each cell was classified on every date: open water (HH below −15 dB) and flooded forest (tree cells, from ESA WorldCover, with HH at or above −5 dB, plus a strict −3 dB version).
  4. We built a time series of areas, a time-colour composite, and a “time under water” map.
  5. We compared NISAR with Sentinel-1 radar and cloud-covered Sentinel-2 photos from the same week.

Key results
• Flooded forest grew about 8× from 19 June to 30 August (39 → 311 km²).
• Open water grew 72% from 19 June to 17 October (611 → 1,050 km²).
• The flood under the trees peaked 5–7 weeks before the open-water flood.
• The HH–HV gap over forest rose from 4.9 to 7.7 dB as water arrived: the double-bounce signature.
• 84% of the forest in the study area (452 of 540 km²) flooded at least once.

Benefits and intended impact
Tonle Sap’s flooded forest is the nursery for about 600,000 tonnes of fish a year, and it has shrunk by about 31% since 1993. Our maps show where and for how long the forest was actually under water, even under cloud. Fisheries managers can estimate nursery habitat, conservation teams can protect the forest that really floods, and disaster agencies can track water reaching rice fields. Repeated every year with free NISAR data, the method can flag weak-flood years early.

Tools and technologies
Python (earthaccess, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, matplotlib, odc-stac, pystac-client); MapLibre GL and Chart.js for the web map; Microsoft Planetary Computer for Sentinel and WorldCover data; GitHub and Vercel for hosting. Code is open source (MIT): https://github.com/afk-2/tonle-sap-invisible-flood

What makes it creative
It tells a story with radar: the flood is invisible to cameras, so we show what NISAR alone can see. A slider, a play-through of the season and click-to-inspect let non-experts explore real radar measurements.

What we considered
We state our limits openly: one season of data only (NISAR data here start in June 2026), an instrument gap from 26 July to 17 August, provisional calibration for most dates, thresholds taken from published values rather than field checks, and 2021 land-cover labels. We report both forest thresholds so the trend can be judged independently of the exact km².

Our hypothesis for the pattern: the Mekong's monsoon rise reverses the Tonle Sap River and refills the lake. The water first spreads under the forest canopy, giving a bright double bounce. As it keeps rising, it covers low trees and shrubs completely, and they switch from bright to dark like open water. That is why flooded forest falls after late August while open water keeps growing into October.
